# Why does the rainbow appear in that shape?

For a rainbow to form, certain conditions are necessary: ​​humid air, that is, full of small droplets; that the sun is clear; but also that the sun is in a certain position so that its rays reach the droplets at a certain angle.

- Why does a rainbow appear in a certain shape?

**Question:** María Fernanda Murillo, 12 years old.

**Answered by:** Ana María Jaramillo, communications assistant, Children's University.

**Source:** Luciano Ángel, PhD in Exact Sciences.

Rainbows have a characteristic and special arc shape. But why do they have this appearance and not be straight or spiral?

Try to remember the last time you saw a rainbow. It was probably around four or five in the afternoon, it had rained, and the sky was starting to clear.

For a rainbow to form, certain conditions are necessary: ​​the air must be humid, that is, full of small droplets; the sun must be clear so that its rays reach the water droplets directly; but also the sun must be in a certain position so that its rays reach the droplets at a certain angle.

So, if you're looking for a rainbow, look east on a rainy afternoon, when the sun starts to peek through the clouds. Or east on a rainy morning.

But why does the rainbow have that shape? Sunlight contains all colors, and a drop of water has the property of breaking that light down into rays of each of those colors.

According to this theory, each raindrop produces a rainbow, but why do we see large bands of color instead of millions of tiny rainbows? The answer lies in the angle at which the colored rays emerge from each raindrop.

We already mentioned that the angle at which sunlight enters raindrops is important for a rainbow to form. But we also need to know that each color of light has a different frequency. Because of this frequency, the colored rays that strike the raindrop are reflected at different angles.

[![Image of how light reflects inside a drop of water](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/35964465-5bc6-4bea-aa14-d6dc3210db25/web/Gota%20de%20lluvia.png)](https://www.eafit.edu.co/sistema-ciencia-tecnologia-innovacion/universidad-ninos/red-preguntas/tierra-y-medio-ambiente/por-que-se-da-la-forma-del-arcoiris)

![](https://www.eafit.edu.co/sistema-ciencia-tecnologia-innovacion/universidad-ninos/red-preguntas/tierra-y-medio-ambiente/por-que-se-da-la-forma-del-arcoiris)

[![Image of colored waves](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/ea580514-0c53-4698-a505-0fd8fe172879/web/ondas-colores.png)](https://www.eafit.edu.co/sistema-ciencia-tecnologia-innovacion/universidad-ninos/red-preguntas/tierra-y-medio-ambiente/por-que-se-da-la-forma-del-arcoiris)

![](https://www.eafit.edu.co/sistema-ciencia-tecnologia-innovacion/universidad-ninos/red-preguntas/tierra-y-medio-ambiente/por-que-se-da-la-forma-del-arcoiris)

This means that only one of the rays coming out of each drop reaches our eyes, and that we see only one color in it, and in all those that receive the sun's rays at the same angle, the same color.

Now, if we could extend a thread from the sun to each of the raindrops we see, and from there to our eyes, we would notice that those raindrops where the angle between the ray coming from the sun and the ray going to our eyes remains the same are positioned in an arc in front of us. Therein lies the key to the shape of the rainbow: each of the colored arcs we see is formed by the raindrops where the incoming and outgoing light rays form the same angle.

But there's something more: when the sun's rays enter the drops at a certain angle, they can bounce twice inside them (just like a billiard ball); then, the colored rays are reversed and we can see, higher up, a second rainbow with the colors reversed.

It's like they say: it all depends on the angle from which you look at it.

For the more curious…

Where does the rainbow form? Why does it always seem to be the same distance away?

Actually, it's not at a specific distance. The light reaches us from droplets located at different distances, but we don't focus on each droplet individually, nor on the droplets at a particular distance; rather, we somehow see them all at once.

When we observe a rainbow, we do so in the same way as when we look very far away (at the stars or the horizon), with relaxed vision, with our gaze lost in infinity.
